source.title: RefusalGuard: Geometry-Preserving Fine-Tuning for Safety in LLMs

record.tranche_reason: The paper analyzes refusal using a low-dimensional cone and reports its coordinate statistics and changes under fine-tuning. This is a refinement of the single-direction account, but the paper does not itself test a single difference-in-means direction by ablating or adding it.
record.gate_note: The paper's discussion of earlier work and its claims that refusal is not a single isolated feature are not counted as results by themselves. Its own cone-coordinate and per-layer geometry measurements bear on V4. It does not apply the original difference-in-means measurement or removal/addition intervention, test a weight edit or jailbreak that suppresses the direction, separate harmfulness judgment from refusal, test transfer, or study alignment training for existence of a removable direction.
record.test_reason: The paper adopts a k-dimensional refusal cone from prior work (Wollschläger et al. 2025) as a fixed tool and uses it to regularize ReFT fine-tuning. Its results are its own method's safety and utility against LoRA, CB and RepBend, plus geometry metrics tracked under fine-tuning. It never compares a cone with a single difference-in-means direction. It never ablates or adds the direction or cone to show mediation, and never tests whether multiple directions are needed. The Table 15 cone-coordinate means are descriptive: the cone basis, k and the extraction procedure are not specified, so the numbers cannot show refusal is better described as a cone. Fine-tuning-induced geometry drift tracking ASR is a related but different construct and is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that fine-tuning, including just 10 harmful examples or benign GSM8K/MedQA/OpenOrca data, degrades refusal. They attribute this to directional drift, cone distortion and task-safety interference. RefusalGuard, a ReFT variant penalizing updates inside the refusal subspace, keeps ASR near base levels across Gemma, LLaMA and Qwen models with modest utility loss. The cone framing is taken from prior work, not established by the paper.
record.recipe_differences: The study identifies and tracks a low-dimensional refusal cone, then constrains representation-fine-tuning updates projected into that subspace. It does not use the original difference-in-means direction ablation/addition procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Per-layer statistics differ across layers; the paper says degradation is strongest in mid-to-late layers. Geometry preservation and safety outcomes also vary with the fine-tuning method and geometry-preservation coefficient.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning moves harmful-prompt activations away from the base refusal cone (LLaMA-3.1-8B). Under standard fine-tuning, alignment falls from 0.91 to 0.63 and cone drift rises from 0 to 0.31, while ASR rises from 0.07 to 0.41 (Table 13). Penalizing cone-parallel updates keeps ASR near base levels across 5 models (Tables 2, 3, 5, 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning degrades refusal by displacing and distorting the refusal subspace; constraining updates within that subspace preserves refusal.

record.peer_reviewed: COLM 2026 (stated as published as a conference paper)
record.problems: The reported geometry measurements are for LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct in the cited tables and do not causally test whether any cone coordinate is necessary or sufficient for refusal. The paper does not report uncertainty estimates for the listed results.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows from the per-layer geometry results in Table 16 or the cone-coordinate results in Table 15 were left out. Other fine-tuning dynamics tables and behavioral benchmark results were not recorded because they do not test whether refusal is better characterized by multiple directions than by one direction.

untested.parts: No comparison of a cone or multiple directions against a single direction or an affine account. No ablation or addition of cone directions, and no necessity or sufficiency test. The cone is assumed from prior work.
RefusalGuard preserves refusal geometry during fine-tuning but does not train against direction ablation and does not test attacks suppressing the direction.
Studies post-alignment fine-tuning drift, not how alignment training determines whether one removable direction exists.

record.verdict_notes: The cone extraction procedure and the dimension k are never specified. Mechanistic tables are LLaMA-3.1-8B only and report no uncertainty. Several values are suspiciously round (e.g. ProjMag exactly 1.00 at checkpoint 0, coordinate means about 0.25 each). The paper is a T4 method paper; the reader's 'supports V4' label is unwarranted, because the study assumes rather than tests the cone account.

versions.untested_parts: No difference-in-means direction is extracted and ablated or added; refusal behavior after those interventions and preservation of other abilities are not tested.
No weight edit or abliteration is tested.
No attack is tested as suppressing the direction, and no training against its ablation is performed.

The paper does not directly compare a cone or multiple directions with a single direction or an affine model in a causal refusal intervention; its coordinate and geometry measurements are not a test of necessity or sufficiency.
The paper reports harmfulness and refusal metrics but does not test whether harmfulness judgment is encoded separately from refusal.
No cross-language transfer or transfer between base and instruction-tuned variants is tested.
The paper studies downstream fine-tuning effects on refusal geometry, but does not test how or when alignment training creates or fails to create a removable direction.

relation.reason: The refusal cone is estimated once from the aligned model, held fixed, and used as a tool: as the regularizer's subspace and as the reference for the drift metrics. Whether it mediates refusal is never tested.

tranche.reason: The study takes a refusal cone from prior work as given (extraction method and k not stated) and uses it to regularize ReFT. It reports its own method's ASR and utility against LoRA, CB and RepBend, plus correlational geometry metrics. It has no ablation or addition test, no single-direction vs cone comparison, and no cone-dimension results, although it says it varied the cone dimension.

source_check.notes: Tables 13-16 cover LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct only and are correlational, under 10-example harmful fine-tuning per Sec 2.3. Table 15 implies k=4, and the layer-16 values in Table 16 match the checkpoint-1000 values in Tables 13/14. All rows' V4 links are doubtful and should probably be "none". The text never states how the cone is extracted, so the pack's claim that it is "not difference-in-means" cannot be checked.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Cone-coordinate statistics for aligned, standard ReFT, and RefusalGuard checkpoints on LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports four separate cone-coordinate means and entropy/top-1 concentration measures; it describes standard fine-tuning as concentrating the profile and RefusalGuard as preserving broader support (R01-R18). This supports a cone-based description, without demonstrating causal necessity.
